methods.quote: we estimate the threshold $\hat\tau = \Phi^{-1}(1-\hat p)$ from the binary marginal, then maximize the conditional log-likelihood ... over $\rho$ (`polyserial_corr`, `src/syntha/generator/copula.py`)
methods.evidence: src/syntha/generator/mixed_corr.py polyserial_correlation does NOT perform numerical MLE over rho. It uses the closed-form normal-scores point-biserial estimator: rho = r_pb * sqrt(p(1-p)) / phi(tau). No log-likelihood is constructed; no optimization is performed. Also the function is named `polyserial_correlation` (not `polyserial_corr`) and lives in mixed_corr.py (not copula.py).
methods.replacement: we estimate the threshold $\hat\tau = \Phi^{-1}(1-\hat p)$ from the binary marginal, rank-transform $y_i$ to normal scores $z_i = \Phi^{-1}((\mathrm{rank}(y_i)-0.5)/n)$, and use the closed-form biserial-style estimator $\hat\rho = r_{pb}\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)}/\varphi(\hat\tau)$, where $r_{pb}$ is the Pearson correlation between $z_i$ and $x_i$ (`polyserial_correlation`, `src/syntha/generator/mixed_corr.py`). This is exact when the latent-bivariate-normal assumption holds and avoids the cost of full MLE.

methods.quote: For binary–binary pairs we solve the tetrachoric estimating equation by Brent bisection on $[-0.999, 0.999]$, evaluating the BVN-CDF with the Drezner & Wesolowsky 1990 8-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature (with the $|\rho|$-branched kernel of [13]) and applying the Bonett–Price small-sample correction [12] (see `tetrachoric_corr` and `_drezner_bvn_cdf` in `src/syntha/generator/copula.py`).
methods.evidence: src/syntha/generator/mixed_corr.py: (1) function is `tetrachoric_correlation` in mixed_corr.py, not `tetrachoric_corr` in copula.py; (2) helper is `_bvn_cdf` not `_drezner_bvn_cdf`; (3) the docstring of _bvn_cdf cites Drezner 1978, not Drezner & Wesolowsky 1990; (4) there is NO |ρ|-branched kernel — a single arcsin/Gauss-Legendre branch is used unconditionally; (5) NO Bonett–Price small-sample correction is applied anywhere — the function just brentq-solves the BVN tail equation. `grep` for 'Bonett' returns hits only in docs/ROADMAP and the docstring header, never in implementation code.
methods.replacement: For binary–binary pairs we solve the tetrachoric estimating equation by Brent's method on $[-0.999, 0.999]$ (`scipy.optimize.brentq`, xtol $10^{-5}$), evaluating the bivariate-normal CDF with an 8-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature of Drezner's 1978 arcsin transform (see `tetrachoric_correlation` and `_bvn_cdf` in `src/syntha/generator/mixed_corr.py`). The Bonett–Price small-sample correction is not currently applied; at the n>10^4 cohort sizes used here the unadjusted ML estimate is essentially unbiased.

methods.quote: $\hat R$ is projected to a valid correlation matrix by clipping negative eigenvalues to $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$, reconstructing, and rescaling to unit diagonal via $D^{-1/2}\tilde R D^{-1/2}$ (Higham 2002 [28]); PSD-ness is verified by a second eigendecomposition.

However, it does NOT perform a second eigendecomposition to verify PSD-ness afterwards — there is no verification step. It is also a single eigenvalue-clip projection, not Higham's alternating-projection algorithm.
methods.replacement: $\hat R$ is projected to a valid correlation matrix by symmetrizing, clipping negative eigenvalues to $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$, reconstructing, and rescaling to unit diagonal via $D^{-1/2}\tilde R D^{-1/2}$ (`_nearest_psd`, `src/syntha/generator/copula.py`). This is a single-pass eigenvalue-clipping projection rather than Higham's alternating-projection algorithm [28]; the Cholesky step at sample time fails fast if the result is not PSD.

methods.quote: A Poisson encounter process (mean configurable) generates two to four additional encounters per patient with shared `HASTA_ID`, age-advance per offset, and sticky comorbidity flags. Per-lab time series are reconstructed by an autoregressive-order-one (AR(1)) process $X_t = \mu_t + \phi(X_{t-1} - \mu_{t-1}) + \varepsilon_t$ with default $\phi = 0.7$, $\mu_t$ encoding any secular trend, and $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.
methods.evidence: src/syntha/longitudinal.py TrajectoryConfig.encounters_per_patient_mean defaults to 4.0 (Poisson mean), not 'two to four'. The lab time-series in `_ar1_path` (src/syntha/longitudinal_labs.py) is NOT an AR(1) with autoregressive coefficient phi — it is an unconditional random walk: `current = current + noise + trend` (i.e. phi is implicitly 1). There is no parameter phi=0.7 anywhere in the code (`grep -n 'phi' src/syntha/longitudinal*.py` returns no results).
methods.replacement: A Poisson encounter process (default mean = 4 encounters over a configurable history window) generates additional encounters per patient with shared `HASTA_ID`, age-advance per offset, and sticky comorbidity flags. Per-lab history is reconstructed by a backward random walk anchored at the latest value, $X_{t-1} = X_t + \varepsilon_t - \mathrm{trend}\cdot\Delta t$, with $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ and column-specific $\sigma$ taken from clinical biological-variation tables (`COLUMN_DRIFT`, `src/syntha/longitudinal_labs.py`).

nshadow_verification.suggested_replacement: The `syntha audit` command runs (i) a Stadler-style nearest-synthetic-neighbor MIA and (ii) a logistic-regression train-on-synthetic / test-on-real-holdout attribute-inference attack (AIA) on sensitive targets (hypertension [Hipertansiyon], diabetes [DM_Tum], hyperlipidemia [Hiperlipidemi]). The CI gate (`.github/workflows/privacy-audit.yml`) seeds `numpy.random.default_rng(42)`, splits the input 80/20 into train/holdout, fits `GaussianCopulaGenerator(random_seed=0)` on the training fold, samples a synthetic cohort of the same size as the training fold, computes Euclidean nearest-neighbor distances on StandardScaler-standardized features, and fails the build if MIA AUC exceeds `syntha.privacy.DEFAULT_MIA_THRESHOLD = 0.60` (AIA threshold 0.70). The audit runs once per CI invocation against the committed sample (`examples/sample_output/sample_episodes.csv`); no shadow-model ensemble or multi-replicate procedure is configured.

Changes in hypertension prevalence, awareness, treatment, and control rates in Turkey from 2003 to 2012. J Hypertens. 2016;34(6):1208-1217. doi:10.1097/HJH.0000000000000901. PMID: 26991534.
patent2.reported_prevalence: Approximately 30% (described in the paper and follow-up commentary as stable at ~30% across PatenT 2003 and PatenT-2 2012; the 30% claim in the manuscript is accurate).

tekharf.reported_hyperlipidemia_prevalence: TEKHARF is a real long-running cohort (Onat et al., from ~1990 onwards) with many publications, but no single canonical paper I can verify reports the specific '>40% above age 40' figure used in the manuscript. The closest verifiable TEKHARF-linked figures are LDL-C >=130 mg/dL of 30.5% (men) and 38.1% (women) in adults >30 (cited via Sozmen et al. Anatol J Cardiol 2016;16(6):370-384) — close to but not exactly '>40% above age 40'. Pinning a single Vancouver citation to the manuscript's specific claim would risk fabrication.

tr_primary_care_depression.reported_prevalence_range: Recent population-based Turkish Health Survey data (2016, 2019) report depressive-symptom prevalence of ~6.3-9% (Ministry of Health), not the 10-20% range claimed in the manuscript. While some Turkish primary-care or specialty-population studies have reported figures in the 10-20% range, the literature is fragmented across many small studies and there is no single canonical citation that anchors '10-20% in Turkish primary care' with high confidence.

tr_epi_verification.rewritten_limitations_sentence: (i) Synthetic disease prevalence is substantially below Turkish epidemiologic estimates by construction of the data-quality-curated source — for example, diabetes mellitus is ~4.8% in syntha v0.5.x versus 13.7% in TURDEP-II [33], and hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and depression are similarly under-represented relative to national figures. This is expected: the pristine cohort used as the generative substrate was curated for data quality rather than to be marginally representative of the Turkish adult population. Consequently, risk-prediction models trained on syntha v0.5.x **must** be recalibrated against TÜİK and TURDEP-II marginals (and, where relevant, condition-specific national surveys) before any deployment; uncalibrated use will systematically underestimate absolute risk.
